_comment: Facts a correct handling of this call has to reach the caller. End-state
checking cannot see these: the database is identical whether or not the agent
told him how much the overnight traffic actually was, how little was left
before he bought anything, that none of it can be given back, or that the
plan slows down rather than billing him for it. This call is handled badly if
any of them goes unsaid - he rang up believing he had been hacked and
believing he was about to be charged for it.
Each entry is satisfied when any one of its surface forms appears in the
agent's utterances, matched case-insensitively with whitespace collapsed. The
A form that is a single number or a single word is matched on boundaries; a
form of two or more words is matched as a plain substring. That is why bare
figures like '15' are listed: '15' will find "15 USD", "15.00 dollars" and
"a total of 15", but will not match '$150', so an agent that quotes the wrong
amount gets no credit. Bare words are fenced for the same reason - 'two' must
not be found inside 'network'. Anchors are only ever the whole value: 'five'
is not listed for 95, since "five business days" would then satisfy a fee.
alternatives exist so an agent is not failed for saying 'forty dollars'
instead of '$40'. Facts the records already carry are not repeated here as
speech - that the line ends the cycle with 7.2 gigabytes of high-speed data
and that five gigabytes were added is checked as state.

required.why: he was asleep and did not believe the alert; the carrier's own measured figure for the window is the evidence that the usage was real, and it is what his handset's app screen gets corroborated against

he is travelling before the cycle ends and has to decide whether to spend forty dollars; what is actually left at full speed is the number that decision turns on, and it is not the number the alert gave him

he asked outright whether the data was coming back, and turning off the app setting feels to him like undoing it; no tool credits metered usage, and letting him believe otherwise is a promise the carrier cannot keep
he was braced for a surprise bill; what the plan actually does past the allowance is slow him down, and the current bill carries no overage - both are things he can only learn by being told

the policy forbids quoting a price that has not been read from a current offer, and he has to authorise the exact amount before it is charged; forty dollars is the figure he objected to and then agreed to
the charge does not come out now, it lands on a bill he has not received yet, and he needs to know it is a single charge on that bill rather than a new monthly cost
